title: Bank of Canada expects 2nd round of oil-linked inflation in 2027, Macklem says
summary: Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem sees high energy prices continuing to sting consumers at the fuel pump and beyond in 2027, even as oil prices fall from recent peaks.

image.caption: Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem, seen here in Ottawa on Oct. 28, said Tuesday that oil shock linked to the war in the Middle East will stoke inflation again next year. (The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Business·New
Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem sees high energy prices continuing to sting consumers at the fuel pump and beyond in 2027, even as oil prices fall from recent peaks.
Says central bank is bracing for 'larger and more frequent supply shocks'

In a speech on Tuesday, he warned a second round of the recent oil shock linked to war in the Middle East will stoke inflation next year. His remarks dampen expectations that a recent decline in benchmark oil prices would yield meaningful relief for consumers and businesses.
"This second-round effect of the oil shock will add to inflation persistence," he said at an event hosted by the Economic Club of Canada, in Toronto on Tuesday.
"Historical lags and our own business surveys suggest more pass-through to the consumer in the year ahead."
Macklem added that so far, businesses have largely absorbed higher production and transportation costs linked to high energy prices.

The October inflation data from Statistics Canada gave little evidence of high oil prices spilling into other segments of the economy. The consumer price index rose 3.1 per cent on a year-over-year basis last month, matching a 3.1 per cent increase in September.
Last month, the Bank of Canada hiked its policy interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.5 per cent, ending a year-long pause at 2.25 per cent with its first increase since 2023.
Tiff Macklem on what might prompt another rate hike

In their summary of deliberations published on Nov. 10, policymakers said further hikes may be needed as high oil prices and rising business costs collide with a resilient economy, risking broad-based inflation through 2027.

In its October Monetary Policy Report, the Bank of Canada called for inflation to remain near three per cent through much of 2027. At the time, policymakers said they expect prices to ease toward two per cent, the mid-point of the central bank's target range, in 2028.

Since then, global oil benchmarks have fallen to roughly three-month lows, due in part to potential military de-escalation between the United States and Iran. The situation has been helped by rising exports of Middle Eastern oil to global markets through the Strait of Hormuz, the vital shipping route that’s been heavily disrupted by the conflict.
Looking ahead, Mackelm said the Bank of Canada is preparing to respond to "larger and more frequent supply shocks."
"Inflation is likely to be pushed off course more frequently and for longer," he said on Tuesday.

"Monetary policy can’t lower global energy prices. But it can limit how much they spill over. Our goal is to avoid a situation where Canadians face rising prices for a wide range of goods and services."
The Bank of Canada is scheduled to make its final rate decision of 2026 on Dec. 9.

Its governing council will have two fresh economic data points to consider ahead of that meeting. Statistics Canada is scheduled to release its gross domestic product reading for the third quarter on Nov. 30, followed by the November Labour Force Survey on Dec. 4.

Tuesday’s speech is one of Macklem's first major public appearances since announcing earlier this month that he will not seek a second term, and will step down when his seven-year mandate expires on June 2.
